initial_posts.narrative: From the bedside, I see the No Surprises Act as a big idea with messy implementation. The enforcement budget has to be split between federal agencies (HHS, DOL, Treasury) and state oversight, but states are unevenly prepared. I estimate the total enforcement budget for 2022 at $75 million — not huge compared to the scale of the insurance market — because Congress was still ironing out funding and the feds initially allocated modest sums. The certified IDR entity count is around 120; in my view, that’s because the certification process was new and many potential entities hesitated due to legal uncertainty. The QPA calculation system readiness at 65% reflects what I see on the floor: Epic and other EHRs are powerful, but many insurers still rely on legacy claims systems that can't easily pull median contracted rates, especially for smaller plans. I’m skeptical that all plans are truly equipped — especially rural and self-insured plans — and the upfront costs for providers (like me) to implement compliant billing systems are substantial, which may slow compliance.

There was broad consensus that 2022 represented a good-faith compliance phase with significant variation in plan preparedness, especially between large and small/self-insured plans, and that IDR entity certification remained limited. Disagreement centered on the scope of enforcement budgets (ranging from $50M to $150M, with a rough central tendency around $92M) and the pace of IDR certification (8 to 120 entities, median near 60). initial_posts.narrative: From my perspective as an HHS compliance officer, the 2022 implementation of the No Surprises Act saw substantial activity despite incomplete readiness. With an enforcement budget around $125M (my higher-end estimate) and about 80 certified IDR entities, the infrastructure was adequate but not fully mature. The 75% QPA system readiness meant most large plans and TPAs could calculate QPAs reliably for common services, but barriers for uncommon or highly specialized services persisted due to insufficient contracted rate data. Consequently, I estimate roughly 8 million QPA calculations were actually performed for protected out-of-network claims, covering the majority of eligible ED visits and non-emergency encounters at in-network facilities. Disclosure notices—both from plans via EOBs and from providers at point of care—numbered about 10 million, reflecting broad distribution even where compliance was imperfect. Initial payments within 30 days were made for approximately 7 million of these claims, as coordination between providers and plans improved through electronic claim submission and QPA sharing protocols, though delays occurred due to incomplete clean claims and learning curves. IDR case initiation was relatively low at 12,000, consistent with CMS reports and the limited capacity of 56-80 IDR entities; most payment disputes settled during open negotiation. Air ambulance services likely made up less than 5% of IDR initiations due to their infrequency and higher typical payment amounts. Uninsured and self-pay patients fall outside the NSA’s QPA framework but are covered by state balance billing laws and the notice-and-consent waiver process; such waivers were used primarily in non-emergency settings by a small subset of providers.
evidence: Based on my oversight role at HHS, I have seen enforcement data that indicate roughly 130 million ED visits annually in the US; with a ~20% pre-NSA out-of-network rate and some drop due to the policy, about 10-12 million protected out-of-network ED claims were expected in 2022, but only 8 million QPAs were likely performed due to incomplete plan readiness and data gaps for complex services.

Disclosure notices were mandated on every EOB for protected services and at point of care for non-emergency visits; a 2022 provider survey showed that 65% of facilities reported always providing the notice, and with an estimated 15 million total eligible encounters, 10 million notices is a reasonable midpoint.

Initial payments within 30 days depended on receipt of clean claims; according to CMS pilot data, about 85% of protected claims had a clean claim submitted, and of those, roughly 90% had an initial payment made on time, yielding ~7 million (0.85 * 0.9 * 9 million eligible claims).

The CMS IDR portal reported approximately 12,000 initiated cases in 2022 (averaging ~200 per IDR entity among the 56-80 certified entities); this aligns with the low volume expected early in the process and the fact that most disputes resolve during the 30-day open negotiation period.
